267.title: Hildegard of Bingen
267.hook: abbess, composer, healer: she saw God's greening power in all living things
267.howItsDone: Christians and others sing Hildegard's music and read her visions, and some find in her idea of viriditas a way to see God's life in the natural world; Catholics keep her feast day on September 17.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ora et labora, pray and work, Benedict's Rule in three words. Your line was pray and work. Which task did you do slowly? Day two hundred sixty-seven.

The first warm week of spring arrives, and the whole world seems to have turned on overnight. The trees are suddenly hazy with new leaves, the grass is a green so bright it almost hurts, and even the weeds in the sidewalk cracks look proud of themselves. Something is pushing up out of everything. In a German convent long ago, a nun gave that pushing a name. She was a composer, a healer, a writer of visions, a letter-writer to emperors and popes. And she believed the green in the grass was saying something about God. Today's word: viriditas.
screen: `THE FIRST WARM WEEK.` → `EVERYTHING PUSHING UP.` → `A NUN GIVES IT A NAME.`

segments.voice: Hildegard of Bingen was born in the Rhineland. As a child she was given to a monastery, and she lived her whole life in a Benedictine community, the kind of life we met yesterday. By her own account she had seen visions of light since she was small, but told almost no one. Then, in her early forties, she says she heard a command to write down what she saw. She hesitated, doubting herself, and fell ill, and only recovered once she began to write. The book became Scivias, Know the Ways. After that, she seemed to do everything. She founded her own convent. She wrote music that is still sung and recorded today, soaring chants, and a sung drama about the virtues. She wrote about plants and medicine and the human body. She wrote letters to bishops, abbots, emperors and popes, and wasn't shy about telling them what she thought. Running through all of it is one Latin word: viriditas. It comes from viridis, green. Greenness. For Hildegard, it meant the life force of God flowing through creation, the sap in the tree, the health in a body, the freshness in a soul. When a person was dry and tired inside, she described it as losing their greenness. When grace moved in them, they grew green again. It's a picture Christians find in the Bible too, the righteous like a tree planted by the rivers of water, whose leaf does not wither. For Hildegard, the green outside and the life of God inside were not two different things. In 2012, Pope Benedict XVI named her a Doctor of the Church, a title the Catholic Church gives to teachers whose writing it holds up for the whole church.
screen: `A CHILD GIVEN TO A MONASTERY.` · `WRITE WHAT YOU SEE.` · `VIRIDITAS: GREENNESS.` · `A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch something green. A houseplant, a leaf outside the door, the herbs in the kitchen, a blade of grass. If nothing green is near, picture one clearly. Feel it: cool, alive, a little soft. Something in it is still pushing, still growing, even now. Breathe with it. Then ask gently: where in me feels dry right now? If you pray, you can offer that dry place. The bell holds the time.
Viriditas. Latin: greenness. Hildegard's word for God's life pushing up through everything that lives.
Your line: the greening. Today, every time you see something green, let it remind you of Hildegard's word: greenness, still pushing up. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

268.title: Bernard's four loves
268.hook: Bernard of Clairvaux: we love ourselves, then God for our sake, then God for God's sake
268.howItsDone: Christians, especially in Catholic and monastic traditions, read Bernard's On Loving God as a guide to prayer, and use his four degrees to examine what draws them to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was viriditas, Hildegard's greenness. Your line was the greening. Where did you see life pushing up? Day two hundred sixty-eight.

Someone drives to the airport at midnight to pick up a friend. The friend is grateful, and loves them a little more for it. That's not wrong; love often starts with what someone does for us. But there's another kind too. A woman sits beside an old friend in a hospital, though he no longer knows her name. A father keeps loving a son who never calls. Love that doesn't need a reason. A French monk once mapped out how love grows from the first kind to the second. Today: Bernard's four loves.
screen: `A RIDE AT MIDNIGHT.` → `LOVE WITHOUT A REASON.` → `A MAP OF HOW LOVE GROWS.`

segments.voice: Bernard was the abbot of a monastery at Clairvaux in France, a Cistercian, part of a movement that wanted to live Benedict's Rule more simply and strictly. He preached, wrote, and advised popes. One of his books is short: On Loving God. It opens by saying the reason for loving God is God, and the measure is to love without measure. Then he lays out four steps, four degrees of love. The first: we love ourselves, for our own sake. Bernard doesn't scold this. It's where every human starts. A baby loves itself; it has to. The second: we love God, but for our own sake. We turn to God because we need help, because life gets hard, because God gives us things. Again, Bernard isn't embarrassed by this. It's real love, and honest. The third: we love God for God's sake. After a while, turning to God again and again, something changes. Like a friendship that began with favors and became something else. You start to love God not for what you get, but because God is good, and lovely in himself. And the fourth, which Bernard says is rare in this life: we love even ourselves only for God's sake. We see ourselves the way God sees us, and love ourselves for that reason alone. Elsewhere, preaching on the Song of Songs, Bernard puts love's highest form in a phrase people still repeat in Latin: amo quia amo, amo ut amem. I love because I love; I love so that I may love. Love for love's sake. It needs no payment. It is its own reward.
screen: `THE MEASURE: WITHOUT MEASURE.` · `SELF FOR SELF; GOD FOR SELF.` · `GOD FOR GOD'S SAKE.` · `I LOVE BECAUSE I LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice why you love what you love. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind, someone you love. Gently ask: what do I love them for? Let the honest answers come: what they give me, how they make me feel. That's the first step, and it's fine. Then ask: is there anything I love in them just because it's them? Stay with that. If you pray, you can ask the same about God. The bell holds the time.
Bernard's four loves. Self for self, God for self, God for God, and self for God. Love learning to need no reason.
Your line: love for love's sake. Today, do one loving thing for someone with no chance of it coming back to you. Day two hundred sixty-eight.

269.title: The Canticle of the Sun
269.hook: Francis, nearly blind, praises God for brother sun, sister water, even sister death
269.howItsDone: Christians sing versions of Francis's Canticle, such as the hymn 'All Creatures of Our God and King', and Franciscans pray it as part of their tradition of caring for creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernard's four loves: self for self, God for self, God for God, self for God. Your line was love for love's sake. Did you do something with no return? Day two hundred sixty-nine.

A small hut stands beside a chapel in Italy, around the year 1225. Inside, a man is lying in the dark. His eyes are so diseased that daylight is agony, so they've shaded him from it. He's in constant pain. He sleeps badly; tradition says the mice ran over him at night. He has given away everything he ever owned. And in that hut, half blind, sick, and poor, he writes a song thanking God for the sun. His name is Francis of Assisi. Today: the Canticle of the Sun.
screen: `A HUT IN ITALY, AROUND 1225.` → `DAYLIGHT IS AGONY.` → `A SONG FOR THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Francis was the son of a rich cloth merchant who gave it all up to live in poverty, preach, and care for lepers. By 1225 he was worn out and nearly blind, and near the end of his life he composed this song. He didn't write it in Latin, the church's language. He wrote it in the everyday language of his region, and readers of Italian treasure it as an early poem in their language. It begins with praise to the Most High, and then it goes through creation like a family roll call. Praised be you, my Lord, with all your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who brings the day. For Sister Moon and the stars. For Brother Wind and the air. For Sister Water, who is, he says, very useful and humble and precious and pure. For Brother Fire, beautiful and playful and strong. For our Sister Mother Earth, who feeds us. Notice: brother and sister. Not resources. Not scenery. Family. Francis isn't worshipping the sun. He's praising God for it, or through it; his little word per can mean either. And he treats it as kin. Later he added a verse praising those who forgive for love, and the story goes that he sent friars to sing it to settle a quarrel between the bishop and the mayor of Assisi. And at the very end, knowing he was dying, he added one more: praised be you, my Lord, for our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no one living can escape. Sister death. Not an enemy. Part of the family too. He died soon after. In 2015, Pope Francis took the song's opening words, Laudato si', praised be you, as the title of his letter on caring for the earth.
screen: `IN THE PEOPLE'S LANGUAGE.` · `BROTHER SUN, SISTER WATER.` · `KIN, NOT SCENERY.` · `EVEN SISTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise one element. Choose one: the sun, water, or fire. If you can, go to it. Stand in a patch of light, or run water over your hands, or look at a candle or a stove flame. Feel it on your skin. Think of it for a moment as a brother or sister, not a thing. If you pray, you can use Francis's words: praised be you, my Lord, for sister water. The bell holds the time.
The Canticle of the Sun. Francis's song praising God for brother sun, sister water, and at the last, sister death.
screen: `THE CANTICLE OF THE SUN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: praised be, for sister water. Today, every time you turn on a tap, let it be a tiny thank-you. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

270.title: The cloud of unknowing
270.hook: an unnamed English monk: God is reached by love, not by thinking
270.howItsDone: Many Christians practice a form of silent prayer drawn from The Cloud of Unknowing, often called centering prayer, sitting for twenty minutes or so with a single sacred word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Canticle of the Sun: brother sun, sister water, even sister death. Your line was about sister water. Did a tap become a thank-you? Day two hundred seventy.

Some things you can't think your way into. You can read every book on swimming and still sink the first time you're in the deep end. You can analyze a piece of music bar by bar and never be moved by it. And you can list everything you know about someone you love, and the list is not the love. Sometime in the late 1300s, an English writer whose name we'll never know wrote a small book arguing that God is like that. Not a problem to be solved. Someone to be reached, and not by the mind. Today: the cloud of unknowing.
screen: `BOOKS ON SWIMMING.` → `THE LIST IS NOT THE LOVE.` → `AN UNNAMED WRITER.`

segments.voice: The Cloud of Unknowing was written in Middle English, the English of Chaucer, probably by a priest or monk, maybe a Carthusian. Nobody knows. He wrote it as advice to a younger person who wanted to pray more deeply. Here's his picture. When you turn to God in prayer, you find something like a darkness between you and God. A cloud. You can't see through it with your mind. You'll never figure God out. That's the cloud of unknowing. And behind you, he says, you should put everything else, even good thoughts, even holy thoughts, under a second cloud, a cloud of forgetting. So you sit between two clouds. Then what? He says: you can't think your way through the cloud above you. But you can love your way through it. He pictures love as a sharp dart of longing, aimed up at the cloud. Beat on it, he says, with that longing love, and don't give up. In his own old English, he says God may well be loved, but not thought. By love he can be reached and held; by thinking, never. And his practical advice is lovely. Take a short word, one syllable is best, like God, or love. Fasten it to your heart. When thoughts come crowding in, even clever ones, answer them with that one word and let them drop under the cloud of forgetting. You'll recognize this, maybe, from the desert. It's another way of staying in the cell. In the twentieth century, some Catholic monks drew on this book to teach a way of silent prayer many Christians now call centering prayer.
screen: `AN UNKNOWN WRITER, MIDDLE ENGLISH.` · `A CLOUD ABOVE, A CLOUD BEHIND.` · `A SHARP DART OF LONGING LOVE.` · `ONE SHORT WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one word. Choose a short one. God, or love, or peace. Settle, and breathe. Let the word rest in you. You don't need to think about what it means. When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, even a good idea, don't fight it. Just return to your word, gently, and let the thought slip behind you. Again and again. That's the whole practice. The bell holds the time.
The cloud of unknowing. The darkness no mind can see through, and the longing love that can.
Your line: reached by love. Today, when you catch yourself trying to figure everything out, stop, and say your one short word instead. Day two hundred seventy.

271.title: Julian of Norwich
271.hook: a woman walled into a cell beside a church, who saw sixteen visions of love
271.howItsDone: Christians, Anglican, Catholic and others, read Julian's Revelations of Divine Love, and her cell in Norwich, rebuilt after wartime bombing, is visited today as a place of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cloud of unknowing, and one short word. Your line was reached by love. Did your word help when the thoughts crowded in? Day two hundred seventy-one.

A small room is built onto the side of a church in an English city. Stone walls. One little window looks into the church, so you can see the altar. Another looks out onto the street, so people can come and talk. And a door that, once you've entered, you've promised never to walk out of again. Some traditions describe a bishop's blessing at the door, and prayers much like those at a funeral. For the rest of your life, this is your world. In Norwich, a woman chose that life. Today's word is the name for what she became: anchoress.
screen: `A ROOM ON THE SIDE OF A CHURCH.` → `ONE WINDOW TO THE ALTAR.` → `ONE WINDOW TO THE STREET.`

segments.voice: An anchoress, or for a man an anchorite, was someone who withdrew from the world to live enclosed in a cell attached to a church. The word goes back to a Greek verb meaning to withdraw. It sounds like a prison. But anchorites were often respected and sought after, and the window to the street mattered. People came for advice. We don't even know this woman's real name. She's probably called Julian because her cell was at the Church of Saint Julian in Norwich. What we know comes mostly from her own book. In May 1373, when she was thirty and a half, she was so ill that she and everyone around her thought she was dying. A priest held a crucifix before her eyes. And over the next hours she received a series of sixteen visions, which she called showings. Then she recovered. She wrote them down in a short version. And then she spent years thinking and praying about what they meant, and wrote a much longer one. Near the end of it, she tells us that fifteen years and more after the showings, she finally understood. Here it is in Grace Warrack's 1901 version: "Wouldst thou learn thy Lord's meaning in this thing? Learn it well: Love was His meaning." All sixteen showings, the suffering and the strangeness and the comfort, meant one thing. Love. She wrote in a century of plague and war. She didn't look away from pain. She looked through it, and saw love underneath.
screen: `ANCHORESS: ONE WHO WITHDRAWS.` · `MAY 1373: SIXTEEN SHOWINGS.` · `FIFTEEN YEARS AND MORE.` · `LOVE WAS HIS MEANING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit at the second window. Julian's cell had a window to the altar and a window to the street. Sit where you can see out: a real window, a doorway, or just a street pictured in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Watch whoever passes, or picture the people who might: a neighbor, a delivery driver, a child on the way to school. Hold each one kindly for a moment, the way an anchoress kept her street window open for whoever came. If you pray, you can pray for them as they pass. The bell holds the time.
Anchoress. A woman who withdrew into a cell beside a church, with one window to the altar and one to the world.
Your line: love was his meaning. Today, when something confusing or painful happens, try a question in Julian's spirit: what if love is underneath this somewhere? Day two hundred seventy-one.

272.title: The hazelnut
272.hook: Julian is shown a hazelnut: it lasts because God loves it (Revelations 5)
272.howItsDone: Some readers of Julian keep a hazelnut or a small stone as a reminder of her vision, and some prayer groups hold one in the hand while praying.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was anchoress: Julian, in her cell with two windows. Your line was love was his meaning. Did you look for love underneath something? Day two hundred seventy-two.

There's a photograph of Earth taken from far out in space. A tiny blue dot, smaller than a grain of sand in a sunbeam. Everything you've ever known is on it. Every person you've loved. Every war, every wedding. And it looks so small you could cover it with your fingertip. It can stir wonder, and a little fear. How does something that small and fragile keep going? Centuries before any camera, a woman lying sick in Norwich was shown something like that picture. Not a planet. Something she could hold in her hand. Today: the hazelnut.
screen: `A BLUE DOT FROM SPACE.` → `SMALL ENOUGH TO COVER.` → `SOMETHING IN HER HAND.`

segments.voice: It's in the fifth chapter of Julian's book, early in her showings. She says she was shown a little thing, about the size of a hazelnut, lying in the palm of her hand, round as a ball. Think of it: a hazelnut, the kind you'd crack at Christmas. She looked at it with what she calls the eye of her understanding, and wondered: what can this be? And the answer came, in Grace Warrack's 1901 version: "It is all that is made." Everything. The whole creation. The sky and the sea and every living thing, and Julian herself, the size of a nut in her palm. And her first reaction is close to the blue-dot feeling. She marveled that it could last at all, because it seemed so small it might just fall into nothing. And the answer she was given is the heart of today. It lasts, and always will, because God loves it. That's it. Not because it's strong. Not because it's important. Because it's loved. And then she sees three things in that little nut. God made it. God loves it. God keeps it. Then Julian draws a conclusion. She says we won't find rest in things that are made, because they're so small. We rest only in the one who made them. But she doesn't despise the little nut. It's loved, after all. On an ordinary day, this is a picture you can carry in your pocket. Whatever feels fragile right now, a body, a marriage, a job, the whole world on the news, Julian says the same thing about it: it lasts because it's loved.
screen: `A LITTLE THING IN HER PALM.` · `IT IS ALL THAT IS MADE.` · `IT LASTS BECAUSE GOD LOVES IT.` · `MADE, LOVED, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold something tiny in your palm. A nut, a bean, a pebble, a button, a ring. If you have nothing, cup your empty hand and imagine one. Settle, and breathe. Look at it. Think: this is how small everything is. And then, if it helps, say the three things quietly to yourself: made, loved, kept. Let your hand stay open. The bell holds the time.
The hazelnut. Julian's picture of all creation, tiny in her palm, lasting because God loves it.
Your line: it lasts because it's loved. Today, carry one small thing in your pocket. Each time your hand finds it, remember: made, loved, kept. Day two hundred seventy-two.

273.title: All shall be well
273.hook: Julian heard: all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well (Revelations 27)
273.howItsDone: Some Christians repeat Julian's words in times of grief or fear, and her line is read at funerals, printed on cards, and prayed slowly as a single sentence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hazelnut: all creation in Julian's palm. Your line was it lasts because it's loved. Did your pocket remind you? Day two hundred seventy-three, the end of the week.

It's a question that tends to come at night, after bad news. A diagnosis. A child in trouble. A headline you can't stop thinking about. If God is good, why is there so much wrong in the world? Why didn't God just prevent it? Julian of Norwich asked exactly that, not as a debate but in prayer. She says she wondered why, in God's great wisdom, sin hadn't simply been stopped at the start. And the answer she received has traveled a long way from her small room. Today: all shall be well.
screen: `THE QUESTION AT NIGHT.` → `WHY NOT PREVENT IT?` → `JULIAN ASKED IT TOO.`

segments.voice: It's in chapter twenty-seven of her book. Julian thinks that if only there had never been sin, everything would have been fine. Why allow it? And she hears Jesus answer. First, a strange phrase: sin is behovely, an old word meaning something like fitting, or bound to be. Scholars still discuss exactly what she meant. And then, in Grace Warrack's 1901 version, the famous words: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Notice what the answer doesn't do. It doesn't explain the suffering. It doesn't say the pain isn't real, or that it's secretly good. Julian says plainly that she didn't understand how it could be true. She saw the evil in the world clearly. She even says, later on, that God will do a great deed at the end of time, and that we can't know now what it is or how it will make everything well. So this isn't optimism. Optimism says things will probably work out. Julian's line is something else. As she hears it, even the things that won't work out are held inside a love bigger than they are. And it comes in three beats, like a heartbeat. All shall be well. And all shall be well. And all manner of thing, every kind of thing, shall be well. Centuries later, the poet T. S. Eliot wove her words into his poem Little Gidding. Look back at this week: Hildegard's greening, Bernard's four loves, Francis's family of creatures, the cloud, Julian's cell, her hazelnut. Each of them, in a different way, kept coming back to love.
screen: `WHY NOT PREVENT SIN?` · `SIN IS BEHOVELY.` · `ALL SHALL BE WELL.` · `NOT OPTIMISM: HELD IN LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it once, slowly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that is not well right now. Don't push it away. Hold it honestly. Then, slowly, say Julian's words, aloud or silently: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. Don't force yourself to feel it. Just let the words sit next to the thing that hurts. The bell holds the time.
All shall be well. Julian's answer to why: not an explanation, but a promise that all is held in love.
Your line: all shall be well. Today, when bad news comes, big or small, say it once under your breath, next to the worry, not instead of it. Day two hundred seventy-three.

pairs: at the end, not known now

myth: all shall be well means nothing bad is really happening
Julian saw evil clearly; the promise sits beside the pain, not instead of it.
Julian said she didn't understand how it could be true
she held the promise without a full explanation.
a modern poet wove her words into a famous poem
T. S. Eliot.

fork.setup: you're Julian. you've asked why God didn't simply prevent sin. what kind of answer comes?
options: a promise: all shall be well.
fork.reveal: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." a promise, not an explanation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful don't-worry line.
what it means: evil is real, and not explained; but all things are held in a love that will make them well.
what a scholar hears: chapter 27's 'sin is behovely'; the 'great deed' of chapter 32; and Eliot's use of the line in Little Gidding (1942).

sources.ref: Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 27
